moments.title: A quadratic without real roots
moments.text: The video starts with $x^2-2x+4=0$. Its negative discriminant means it has no real solutions.

moments.title: Extend beyond the real numbers
moments.text: Complex numbers allow the negative discriminant to yield two complex roots.

moments.title: Work with the negative square root
moments.text: The expression $\sqrt{-12}$ is written as $2\sqrt3\,i$, where $i^2=-1$.

moments.title: Introduce the imaginary unit
moments.text: The imaginary unit satisfies $i^2=-1$; here it is used to express the square root of a negative real number.

moments.title: The complex roots
moments.text: The solutions simplify to $1+\sqrt3\,i$ and $1-\sqrt3\,i$.

moments.title: A graph and complex roots
moments.text: The real graph does not cross the real $x$-axis. The presenter refers to a separate visualization of the complex roots.

moments.title: Cartesian form
moments.text: A complex number is written $z=a+bi$, with real part $a$ and imaginary part $b$.

moments.title: Real and imaginary parts
moments.text: For $z=1+\sqrt3\,i$, $\operatorname{Re}(z)=1$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z)=\sqrt3$.

moments.title: The complex plane
moments.text: The presenter introduces the Argand diagram as a way to represent a complex number geometrically.

moments.title: Plot the point
moments.text: Use the real part for the horizontal coordinate and imaginary part for the vertical coordinate; $1+\sqrt3\,i$ is represented by $(1,\sqrt3)$.

notes.title: Complex roots and x-intercepts
notes.text: At the start, roots and x-intercepts are discussed together. Non-real complex roots are not x-intercepts of the usual real graph.
notes.write: A real x-intercept corresponds to a real root. A quadratic can have complex roots while its real graph has no x-intercepts.

moments.title: Operations and representations
moments.text: The video compares addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and powers in Cartesian, polar and exponential forms.

moments.title: Addition and subtraction
moments.text: In Cartesian form, add or subtract real parts and imaginary parts separately.

moments.title: Add two complex numbers
moments.text: The presenter adds $1+\sqrt3\,i$ and $2+2i$, obtaining $3+(2+\sqrt3)i$.

moments.title: Multiplication and division
moments.text: The video explains that several forms can be used, then starts with Cartesian multiplication.

moments.title: Expand the product
moments.text: Multiply the binomials and replace $i^2$ by $-1$, then collect real and imaginary parts.

moments.title: Polar multiplication
moments.text: For nonzero complex numbers in polar form, multiply moduli and add arguments.

moments.title: Divide in Cartesian form
moments.text: Multiply numerator and denominator by the conjugate of the nonzero denominator to obtain a real denominator.

moments.title: Polar and exponential division
moments.text: Divide moduli and subtract arguments; the denominator must be nonzero.

moments.title: Powers
moments.text: The presenter compares repeated Cartesian multiplication with raising the modulus and multiplying the argument in polar form.

moments.title: Raise to the fourth power
moments.text: For $z=2\operatorname{cis}(\pi/3)$, the fourth power is $16\operatorname{cis}(4\pi/3)$.

moments.title: A remark about roots
moments.text: The presenter briefly mentions roots at the end; solving for all complex roots requires accounting for all arguments.

notes.title: Finding all complex roots
notes.text: The closing remark suggests that roots work exactly like taking a fractional power. A complex equation can have multiple roots, so one calculator value is not necessarily the complete solution.
notes.write: When solving $z^n=w$, account for all distinct arguments. Complex roots are not required in the syllabus guidance for AHL 1.13.

moments.title: Calculator settings and operations
moments.text: The video introduces complex-number settings, input, stored values and conversion tools on a TI-Nspire.

moments.title: Choose the output format
moments.text: The presenter contrasts real, rectangular and polar output settings.

moments.title: A non-real calculation
moments.text: The presenter demonstrates why a real-only setting can reject an expression involving $\sqrt{-1}$.

moments.title: Switch to polar output
moments.text: The video shows how the TI-Nspire can display an entered Cartesian number in polar or exponential form.

moments.title: Enter Cartesian, polar and exponential forms
moments.text: The presenter demonstrates input conventions for the three forms.

moments.title: Store a complex number
moments.text: A stored variable can be reused for later calculations and operations.

moments.title: Return to rectangular output
moments.text: The stored value is displayed in rectangular form; the video discusses decimal output.

moments.title: Conversion tools
moments.text: The presenter locates tools for conjugates, components, angle, magnitude and conversions between forms.

moments.title: Keep hand methods and exact forms
moments.text: The presenter recommends remaining proficient with exact algebra as well as calculator approximations.

notes.title: Calculator shown
notes.text: The video uses a TI-Nspire, so its key presses and output behaviour should not be assumed to match the Casio fx-CG50.
notes.write: Check the Casio complex-number and angle settings, and use the output form requested by the question.

ican.text: I can use $i^2=-1$ and write a complex number in Cartesian form $a+bi$.
I can identify the real part, imaginary part, conjugate, modulus and argument of a complex number.
I can add, subtract, multiply and divide complex numbers in Cartesian form, by hand and with technology.
I can plot complex numbers and their conjugates on an Argand diagram.
I can solve a real-coefficient quadratic with a negative discriminant and check its complex roots.
I can use technology to evaluate integer powers in Cartesian form and check the output mode.

ku.text: $i^2=-1$. For $z=a+bi$ with real $a,b$, $\operatorname{Re}(z)=a$ and $\operatorname{Im}(z)=b$. The imaginary part is the real coefficient $b$, not $bi$.
The conjugate of $z=a+bi$ is $\overline z=a-bi$. On an Argand diagram it reflects $z$ in the real axis, and $z\overline z=a^2+b^2=|z|^2$.
The modulus is $|z|=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$. For nonzero $z$, an argument is an angle from the positive real axis to the position vector; account for the quadrant. The argument of zero is undefined.
Add and subtract real and imaginary components separately. For products, expand and replace $i^2$ by $-1$.
For a nonzero complex denominator, multiply the numerator and denominator by its conjugate; the resulting denominator is real and positive.
For a quadratic with real coefficients and negative discriminant, the roots are a non-real conjugate pair. They are not real x-intercepts of the graph.
Use Cartesian output for $a+bi$ when requested. Calculator settings and angle units affect displays; keep exact values when the question asks for them.

misc.better: The imaginary part is the real coefficient: $\operatorname{Im}(z)=-4$.
By definition $i^2=-1$; this sign changes the real part when multiplying.
Keep the real part and reverse only the imaginary sign: $\overline z=3+4i$.

misc.weak: A negative discriminant means a real quadratic has no roots at all.
misc.better: It has no real roots, but it has two non-real complex conjugate roots.

misc.weak: The argument is always $\tan^{-1}(b/a)$ without checking the quadrant.
misc.better: Use the signs of $a$ and $b$ to locate the point. The inverse tangent alone may select the wrong quadrant, and requires care when $a=0$.

misc.weak: The complex roots of a quadratic are x-intercepts on its usual real graph.
misc.better: Only real roots correspond to x-intercepts of the real graph.

terms.text: Give a single expression $a+bi$ with real $a,b$, simplifying all powers of $i$.
Reverse the sign of the imaginary part and preserve the real part.
Use the distance from the origin for the modulus and state an appropriate angle with its convention and units.
Apply the formula or an equivalent method, simplify the complex roots and check them in the original equation.

formula.text: The booklet states the Cartesian form $z=a+bi$ and the discriminant $\Delta=b^2-4ac$.

kq.q: Why is $z\overline z$ always a nonnegative real number?
kq.model: For $z=a+bi$, $(a+bi)(a-bi)=a^2+b^2$, a sum of two nonnegative real squares.

kq.q: Why does multiplying by a conjugate help with division?
kq.model: The denominator $c+di$ multiplied by $c-di$ becomes $c^2+d^2$, which is real and nonzero when the original denominator is nonzero.

kq.q: Why do non-real roots of a real-coefficient quadratic occur in conjugate pairs?
kq.model: Conjugating the equation preserves real coefficients. If one non-real number satisfies the equation, its conjugate satisfies it too.

kq.q: Why must the quadrant be checked when finding an argument?
kq.model: A tangent value can correspond to angles in different quadrants. The signs of the real and imaginary coordinates determine the position of the complex number.
